what: The score combines cheapest-insertion distance with a Clarke–Wright-style consolidation credit: Δ insertion minus twice the candidate’s depot distance. It also rewards a geographically compatible unassigned customer that still fits afterward and mildly penalizes one-step residual-capacity waste. Each call uses O(len(current route) + len(unassigned)) time and O(1) extra space.
why: The consolidation term encourages the farthest-seeded route to absorb customers that yield large shared-depot savings rather than leaving expensive customers to seed later routes. The continuation term promotes spatial chains that are likely to remain coherent under subsequent insertion and 2-opt, while its demand weighting and the residual-gap penalty address heterogeneous demands and capacity pressure. The rule is deliberately local: it does not estimate the remaining solution, solve a packing problem, or predict all effects of later randomized choices and 2-opt, so its coefficients and one-customer capacity lookahead may not suit every instance distribution.
